newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels threaten Kisangani after deadline.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels threaten Kisangani after deadline.

text.p: Zairean rebels threatened to capture the eastern garrison city of Kisangani if government troops ignored a Thursday deadline to give up their weapons.
A U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) plane landed at Kisangani with food, establishing a supply route for up to 80 tonnes of food per day avoiding a heavily defended airport just outside the city.

Asked what would happen if troops ignored a rebel deadline of Thursday to lay down arms, rebel Information Commissioner Raphael Ngenda said in Goma: "We will do something, and possibly it will mean the final blow and we will liberate Kisangani."
Both sides are bracing for a showdown over Kisangani, which has an estimated half a million people and is the northeastern capital on the Zaire river and a major government army base.

WFP spokeswoman Brenda Barton said an Ilyushin-76 cargo plane landed at Kisangani's municipal airport, the first time the agency sent such a big plane there instead of the larger international airport, which has a much longer runway.
"WFP staff reported that the city was calm," she said.

She said the plane had 30 tonnes of food, 75 percent of its capacity, because of worries over whether it could land on such a short runway, and people were ready with buckets of water to throw on its tyres in case they were set ablaze by braking.
"It landed safely and did not apply full brakes," she said. "Tomorrow it will bring in 40 tonnes of food on each of two rotations which is enough to feed 160,000 people for a day."
The Ilyushin-76 last flew into Kisangani's international airport, 17 km (10 miles) outside the city, on February 28 when foreign aid workers were evacuated because of insecurity.

"We chose to use the municipal airport as we wanted to establish it as a corridor and the international airport is highly militarised. It is hard for staff and convoys to travel into town because of many checkpoints on the road," she said.
The food will go to feed some 35,000 displaced people in Kisangani, 100,000 Burundian and Rwandan refugees at Ubundu town to the south and 4,000 refugees at Punia to the southeast.

Rebel radio in Goma on Thursday reported the fall of Kongolo, 700 km (440 miles) to the south, at a crossing on the Zaire river and said rebel forces were close to reaching the diamond-rich opposition heartland of Kasai in central Zaire.
"The town of Kongolo was captured without a fight because soldiers have left to reinforce Kisangani, which is surrounded by the Alliance," the rebel Voice of the People radio said.
But residents of Kisangani, Zaire's third largest city, on Wednesday reported an uneasy calm there, saying any fighting between the army and advancing rebels was out of earshot.
With international pressure spurred on by France growing for some kind of intervention in Zaire, Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo denounced foreign indifference since war in the east began last October.

"I find it regrettable that the international community through the United Nations through the United States and Britain gives the impression that the tragedy unfolding in Zaire doesn't interest them," Kengo told a news conference on Wednesday.
"Perhaps because it is a question of Africans," said Kengo, adding the collapse of Zaire would rebound on the whole region.
The rebels want to topple 66-year-old President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is in Europe where he has spent most of his time since having prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland last August.
